articles.title: Alberta's decisive decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump
articles.summary: The overwhelming vote by Alberta to stay in Canada gives Mark Carney political capital to focus on remaking the country's economy, writes the BBC's Lyse Doucet.
body: "Let's move on": Albertans react to separatist movement referendum results
"Vote like Canada depends on it," Prime Minister Mark Carney declared to cheering crowds in Calgary last week on a stage emblazoned with bright red and white "Forever Canadian" banners.
It's a message that appears to have struck a chord with the electorate, as preliminary results show more than two-thirds of Alberta voters said they want to remain a part of Canada.
But the future of the federation does still rest on its richest province.

Alberta, with most of Canada's proven oil reserves and abundant gas and mineral wealth, is playing a pivotal role in Ottawa's drive to survive a punishing trade war with the US by diversifying trade, strengthening its economy, and forging new alliances on the other side of the world.
Carney, the former central banker who grew up in Alberta, is now Canada's builder-in-chief – at home, and beyond its borders.

Note the emphasis in his first statement after Monday's vote on separation in the province, as soon as the scale of the victory was clear: "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other."
Albertans' overwhelming "yes" to stay in Canada gives him political bricks and mortar, too.
"Don't mess with Canada," warned Thomas Lukaszuk, a former lawmaker whose Forever Canadian campaign played a key role in this referendum's outcome.

Addressing elated supporters in Edmonton, the provincial capital, as the "yes" count for Canada kept tumbling in, Lukaszuk underlined that this vote "will send a very strong message to the rest of the world".
Everyone knows he's talking about the troublesome neighbour to the south – in particular its president, who keeps threatening to turn Canada into the 51st US state.
The same day Albertans were voting on their future in Canada, Trump sent his own signal north at a rally in Kansas ahead of next month's US midterm polls.
"I will let you keep ice hockey, and I will let you keep your 'O Canada' national anthem," he promised before adding: "We're only kidding."
For Canadians, it's no laughing matter.

In the run up to this referendum, Carney reiterated a warning he's often sounded that "there are some outside our borders who are working to break us, so they own us" – even if he didn't spell out who "they" is.

And, in this defining time for the separatist camp, some in their ranks didn't hide their direction of travel. Some of their most prominent leaders admitted they travelled to Washington three times last year to meet US State Department officials and outline what an independent Alberta could offer – including a possible oil pipeline through the US to the Pacific.
But the rest of the world may take only passing notice of what was, for Canada, an historic vote sparking conversations and concerns across the country, from coast to coast to coast.
Mark Carney and Alberta's leader Danielle Smith has worked closely on pushing for an oil pipeline to the west coast from the landlocked province.

"Short of a vote to separate, most foreign governments, with the exception of the United States, have little interest in domestic Canadian politics," says Professor Janice Stein, founding director of the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto.

"Foreign investors are focused on the time it will take to complete major infrastructure projects, a return on investment, and predictable regulations," she explains in a nod to Carney's long list of megaprojects he hopes will eventually turbocharge economic growth. They're all costly; many will take years to build.

An ambitious blueprint already includes a proposed pipeline to the Pacific coast which opens opportunities for Alberta's oil to reach Asian markets – a move which also addresses Alberta's long-standing grievance that its economy has been stifled by federal policies, including environmental regulations.
At a rally in Alberta last week, it was Carney's comment that the pipeline "will reduce our dependence on the United States" that triggered the loudest and longest applause of the night.

After Monday's vote, Carney – the former UN Special Envoy for Climate Action and Finance – pointed to "unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta as its core". Political and economic pressures now seem to eclipse his green credentials.
'Great result for Canada', says Carney as Alberta votes to reject separatism
Huge setback for Alberta's separatist movement after decisive defeat
"Build Canada Strong" has been Carney's mantra ever since he first entered politics, a complete neophyte, at the start of last year.

At home there are possible wide-reaching repercussions from the final tallies in the referendum's nine other questions which dealt with issues ranging from greater provincial powers, the costs of immigration, and potential constitutional changes.
Those results are certain to provoke debate, and deal making or breaking, involving Canada's nine other provinces and three territories. They all have their own grievances, too.

The prime minister has had to defend himself when journalists ask if he is spending too much time on foreign trips with his charm offensive to build new political alliances and trade partnerships, including an unprecedented and still uncertain offer of associate membership of the European Union.

"I can do both and I need to do both," he recently replied with his signature bluntness before listing the more than 16 bills which went through Parliament in the last session dealing with everything from major tax changes, public safety, and the price of fuel.

For now, Carney is riding high in the polls at home – including in Alberta, which doesn't traditionally support his Liberal party - in a long "political honeymoon" other beleaguered politicians would envy.

And the plain-speaking politician's strong and steady response to Trump threats, including retaliatory tariffs, has seen his star rising on the world stage. It's an unexpected turn for a country which has often been missing from top tables and has sometimes even been dismissed as "boring".
The Economist magazine decided to put Carney on their cover, on this week of weeks for Canada, with a perfect red maple leaf between his teeth.
"Mark Carney shows middle powers how to handle a dangerous world," reads one of its headlines, with an article which also focuses on Canada's "vulnerabilities" including Alberta's ballot.
"The broader takeaway from this vote might be that Canadian unity is in fine shape," remarks David Moscrop, political scientist and author of the forthcoming book On Nationalism.
"But what happens after Donald Trump is gone and Canada no longer has a single, bombastic target which drives Canadians to rally around the flag?" he asks.

Carney's decision to recently walk away from trade talks with the US gave rise to another swell of Canadian pride and patriotism. But if this trade war drags on with a country which traditionally takes 70% of Canada's exports, Canadians will feel even greater pain in their daily lives.
But today is a day to vigorously wave the maple leaf flag.
"It's a win for Team Canada and its resilience," commented CBC journalist Janyce McGregor during the public broadcaster's rolling coverage of a vast country of never-ending building issues.

articles.title: Swimmer, 65, killed in shark attack off South Africa's east coast
articles.summary: Janine Lochrenberg, 65, was out on her daily morning swim with her club when she was attacked, her family tell the BBC.
body: Janine Lochrenberg had "a deep affinity with the water" her sister told the BBC
A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.
Janine Lochrenberg was swimming off a beach in KuGompo City (formerly East London) on Tuesday morning when she was attacked.
Witnesses said the 65-year-old was bitten in two places and died before she was brought to shore.
Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal ones since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File.

Lochrenberg was out on a daily morning swim with her local open water swimming club when she was attacked at around 08:00 (06:00 GMT). Fellow swimmers brought her to shore, but it's believed she died before they could get her out of the water.
She was bitten on her thigh and her upper arm, one of her fellow swimmers told the BBC. They also said she had been wearing a magnetic shark repellent band on her ankle at the time.
Lochrenberg's sister Margot said she was holding her sister's head as they brought her to shore but believed she bled out in the water.
She told the BBC that her sister had "loved the water so much" despite knowing there was an "elevated shark presence in East London".
"She'd made peace with that. She had a deep affinity with the water and was a remarkable person," she said.
Barbara Briceland, Lochrenberg's partner, told the BBC the retired medical physicist was a good swimmer, who often swam far out into the breakers, and described her as very brave.
"She was highly intelligent, lots of fun, kind, in a quietish way, thoughtful, well-loved with a love of life."
Briceland added they were looking forward to retirement and were about to leave for a three-week road trip together.
Orient Beach, where the attack took place, has been closed alongside another nearby beach, authorities confirmed.

articles.title: Thursday briefing: The crisis putting maternity units in England at risk of closure
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: rising rates of C-sections, staff shortages and years of unresolved concerns are preventing some hospitals from delivering babies safely
body: Good morning. Over the summer, doctors in the emergency department at the North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple, one of the most remote in the UK, received a crash course on delivering a baby. Their training covered subjects nobody wants to hear about when they’re imminently expecting: shoulder dystocia, postpartum haemorrhage, and neonatal collapse. “I’m hoping that we won’t see such emergencies,” one doctor said. “It’s been an intense time.”

That crash course was necessary because maternity services at the hospital have been indefinitely suspended due to staff shortages. Other remote hospitals across the country are expected to do the same, as NHS trusts struggle to recruit enough staff to safely deliver babies. Earlier this week, the Guardian reported that up to 20 maternity units in England could shut. The story sheds light on a maternity care crisis that has been rumbling on for years, and shows how childbirth has changed dramatically over the last decade.

The Guardian’s health policy editor, Denis Campbell, has been reporting on this story, and has covered nearly every major maternity scandal in the health service’s recent history. In today’s newsletter, he reveals the alarming stakes involved in this one. First, here are the headlines.

Oil | Miatta Fahnbulleh is leaning towards rejecting the giant Rosebank oilfield, the Guardian understands, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners.

Reform UK | Farage’s party has been fined more than £2,000 for failing to declare it was the publisher of campaign material seen by voters – including an additional penalty for failing to pay on time.

Defence | Britain risks failing to deter future Russian aggression in the high north beyond the UK because of shortfalls in the number and availability of Royal Navy submarines and warships, MPs on the defence select committee have said.
Technology| Websites around the globe have gone dark after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web.
Israel | The Washington Post photojournalist who was attacked and seriously injured by Israeli settlers in the West Bank on Friday has described how she was saved with the help of local Palestinians.

Matthew Hopkins, NHS Alliance’s lead director of acute care, recently suggested to Denis that up to 20 of the UK’s 155 NHS maternity units could be at risk of closure. Two units, the one in Barnstaple and another in Yeovil, Somerset, have already suspended maternity services because of staffing shortages, while a hospital in Newry, Northern Ireland, plans to permanently shut down its maternity services.

One reason for these potential closures is that people are having fewer children. The Royal Free hospital in North London recently announced that it was permanently closing its maternity unit because the number of women having babies locally has fallen by almost 30% in the last seven years (four of the area’s primary schools have shuttered during the same period). But the main concern for many units at smaller hospitals in rural and coastal areas is staffing. These are often areas without alternative provision nearby.

At the same time, childbirth has changed. More women than ever are now getting C-sections or having births that require medical intervention from doctors, and smaller maternity units are also grappling with a widespread lack of obstetricians. “If you don’t have enough doctors, you can’t run a service safely, so more and more smaller hospitals are considering losing their maternity units altogether,” Denis says.
Why are more women having C-sections?

The rapid growth of caesareans, both planned and emergency, appears to be one of the primary reasons that some smaller hospitals are considering suspending maternity services. The proportion of births performed by caesarean increased from 31% in 2019 to 45% in 2024, and last year was the first time in England that more babies were born via c-section than “natural” births (a term that many women find pretty grating because it implies there’s a hierarchy between births with medical intervention and those without).

“England’s rate of caesareans is unusually high compared to similar European countries, and all of the experts I speak with think this is just going to keep going up and up,” Denis says. This dramatic rise in caesareans has several causes, including changes in clinical practice designed to reduce the risk to babies and (quite rightly) give women more choice over how they give birth, as well as an increase in pregnancies among women who are over the age of 35 (the average age of parents in England and Wales has been increasing steadily for the last 50 years).

But this isn’t the whole story. Some women are also worried about the type of care they might receive during vaginal births. Successive reviews portray a state of crisis, with burnt-out and exhausted midwives, a growing risk of serious injuries, and women of colour experiencing persistent racism and discrimination. A national review of maternity services in England from 2022 to 2024 by the Care Quality Commission warned that serious harm in maternity care risked becoming the norm.

“There’s real concern among maternity doctors that women are reading endlessly negative headlines about the poor quality of NHS maternity care, which is leading them to ask for C-sections,” Denis says.

As the rate of caesareans increases, trainee midwives are struggling to gain the experience of dealing with more complex births, potentially creating a cycle in which more women end up having caesareans. “Rather than building huge obstetric units and planning for a far higher caesarean rate, which is where we’re currently heading, the NHS should be investing in community-based and continuous midwifery care, alongside excellent obstetric care for women who need it,” Debbie Garrod, a midwife and antenatal educator, tells me.
How is the fear of medical negligence claims affecting childbirth?

Another reason for this rising rate of caesareans is something known as “defensive practice”. This is when doctors, nurses and midwives make decisions to avoid blame or complaints, rather than because those decisions are necessarily in a patient’s best interests.

The cost of settling all outstanding maternity-related claims in England was estimated at £37.5bn last year, nearly two-thirds of the NHS’s total £60bn clinical negligence liabilities bill. It’s a figure that senior MPs have described as “jaw-dropping”. In fact, the bill for maternity negligence claims in England since 2019 could be more than the health service’s budget for newborns during the same period.

“If a baby ends up suffering a catastrophic injury because it was deprived of oxygen for a few minutes during birth, that can cost the NHS £20-30m,” Denis says. “Doctors are so aware of these risks, and of being pilloried with scandals and inquiries, that they often try to take a no-risk approach to childbirth.”
What is the government’s approach?

There have been four inquiries into maternity scandals in England since 2015, one national maternity review led by Valerie Amos, and a further two inquiries led by Donna Ockenden, which are now ongoing. Denis estimates these have made no fewer than 700 recommendations for improving maternity services. “Experience shows that many of these have gathered dust on a shelf, and by almost every metric, maternity care has got worse, not better,” he says.

By all accounts, this shouldn’t be happening. The number of births has decreased significantly since the first of these inquiries was published in 2015, while the number of staff in maternity units has increased. So why is maternity care getting worse? “That’s the big question,” Denis says. “You could give about 65 different answers.” So I pressed him on the most important ones.

Childbirth, he says, has become more complicated, as the NHS has attempted to reduce its risks through measures such as early inductions and increased monitoring. As the population has become less healthy, more women also now have underlying health issues such as diabetes and obesity. Meanwhile, women from poorer backgrounds, and Black and Asian women, continue to experience the worst maternal outcomes, as the Amos review demonstrated.

The government’s maternity and neonatal taskforce is expected to publish an action plan before Christmas, building on the recommendations from the Amos review. “There is great scepticism among maternity doctors about this plan, given how little has changed after previous reviews,” Denis says. “I think it’s going to need the best luck in the world to address this sense of fear and failure.”

“Fahnbulleh minded to reject Rosebank oilfield, sources say”, is the Guardian’s splash today. The Mail’s take is “Pathetic”, and Metro writes “Drill, Andy, Drill!”.

The Telegraph has “Putin’s trawlers spy on Britain”, and the Express writes “‘To deter war Britain must be ready’”. The i Paper leads with “Schools face cutting SEND staff to fund 2026 pay rise for teachers”, and the Times has “Chancellor: I’ll cut cost of business to boost UK”. The FT says “Musk’s vision for SpaceX and Tesla combination welcomed by investors”.
The Sun splashes “Kyle inks it’s all over” and the Mirror, on Prince Harry and William’s rift, has “Ruled out”.
‘Disgraceful’: Jackdaw gasfield approval condemned

Climate campaigners have condemned the UK government’s decision to allow the drilling of the Jackdaw gasfield. Critics argue the move will put climate targets at risk, while failing to reduce energy bills and the cost of living crisis. But there could be a significant victory for green activists when it comes to the much larger Rosebank oilfield, with the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, leaning towards rejecting approval. Michael Safi speaks to environment correspondent Matthew Taylor.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Finally, Lake Windermere might be clean again. After years of being pumped with sewage, a creative solution to remove sewage from England’s largest lake has been agreed by campaigners, the Environment Agency and a local water company. Inspired by the clean-up of Lake Annecy in France, the plan proposes a 12 mile tunnel that will take treated effluent from Windermere to the River Leven or the sea.
