articles.title: Besieged Yemeni city on verge of ‘unmanageable’ crisis, aid workers warn
articles.summary: Water and fresh food running out in Taiz as fighting intensifies and Houthi advance cuts off most supply routes
body: The humanitarian crisis in the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz is becoming unmanageable as the city runs out of water, fuel and fresh food, Oxfam aid workers in the country have warned.

Iran-allied Houthi forces have largely encircled the city of more than 900,000 people, cutting it off from most supply routes. This week, heavy fighting has raged around the city’s old airport, causing extensive damage in a densely populated residential area.

The conflict has intensified since forces loyal to the internationally recognised government and the Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on the Houthi-held airport in Sana’a in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that had largely stopped the fighting.

The UN has called for aid workers to be given access to Taiz. Oxfam in London called for the UK to send extra humanitarian aid to the country. The UK has allocated just £104m in aid to Yemen for each of the next three years, down from the £196m allocated in 2020. US aid to the stricken country has been virtually wiped out, and Germany, another leading funder, has halved its aid programme.
Related: Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthrough

Donor countries have subscribed to only 23% of the cost of the UN humanitarian relief programme for Yemen this year, and pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia – itself cash-strapped by the cost of war – to make up the shortfall. The World Food Programme said wheat flour reserves in the city were nearly exhausted as of mid-October.

On Tuesday the UK government allocated an unspecified sum in extra military help to Saudi Arabia to help protect its airports and infrastructure, but London has yet to decide on whether to back a much more robust military response, including supporting the possible deployment of foreign ground troops to Yemen.
Fatma Jaffar, a Yemen-based advocacy manager for Oxfam, said local staff described an almost total siege of Taiz.

“All the main entrances [to the city] have been blocked. The clashes are continuing and the casualties are very high,” she said. “Even people that have money are not able to buy food. Supplies are becoming very limited in the markets. No fuel has entered Taiz for two or three weeks. Drinking water is a massive issue. Even our staff are struggling to buy water.

“Hospitals are struggling without medicines and a lot of people as a result are dying. Those that have been wounded by missiles – there have been attempts to get them out of the city, but because of the blockade they are not able to transfer anyone. Prices have rocketed.

“Our staff told me that people are even searching for apples right now and they cannot find any fresh fruit, and basic commodities are not found inside the city. Garbage is piling up since they are not able to transfer the waste outside the city. They are trying to burn it, but we can only anticipate there will be diseases such as cholera in the near future. If this goes on much longer and access remains blocked, there will be casualties from missiles, hunger and disease from lack of water right across the city.
“The situation was bad before the escalation – Yemen is one of the poorest countries on Earth – and now it is becoming unmanageable.”
Prices have rocketed: a 20-litre container of petrol that cost about $20 (£15) before the crisis is now worth $80 on the hidden market. Potato prices have doubled.
The Houthi focus on Taiz reflects the city’s strategic importance, but the level of resistance inside the city may swallow the group’s resources, weakening its response elsewhere.
Oxfam has been forced to transfer its limited resources from development to emergency humanitarian work, including offering cash transfers.
The Halo Trust, the world’s largest humanitarian landmine-clearance organisation, said 30 of its staff were among hundreds of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city.

In the Trump administration’s fiscal year 2027 budget request to Congress, the US state department has requested no economic support or development assistance specifically for Yemen. By comparison, the US committed roughly $760m in total aid to Yemen during the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency.

UN diplomats are still mediating between the two sides, but there is no sign that either the Houthis or the internationally recognised government are ready for a ceasefire, let alone a long-term settlement.

articles.title: Israeli military detain US and UK volunteers in West Bank including Democratic NY politician Brad Lander
articles.summary: About 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers held near Nahalin in West Bank and taken to police station
body: The Israeli military has detained about 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including the New York Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander, several rabbis and Israel’s former deputy attorney general.

“I’ve been detained by the IDF, along with a group of rabbis and volunteers,” Lander posted from a bus taking him to a police station. “We were simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nahalin in the West Bank. The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know.”

Lander, who is Jewish and an outspoken critic of the Israeli government, describes himself as a liberal Zionist. He believes in the vision of Israel as a safe, Jewish home, but argues that it cannot be a true democracy while it denies Palestinians their human rights and freedom.
An ally of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, Lander’s critical approach to Israel was a key factor in his resounding primary victory against Dan Goldman, a prominent supporter of Israel.

He condemns Israel’s continued occupation of the West Bank and Gaza, supported the restriction of US military aid to Israel and believes that Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks amounts to genocide.
Settler militants have unleashed extreme violence on Palestinians attempting to harvest olives from their trees across the occupied West Bank, and anyone accompanying them.

A vicious assault on a US photojournalist and attacks on European diplomats and a French mayor over the weekend drew international condemnation and calls for the Israeli government to crack down on militants.
Wednesday’s olive-picking from trees outside the village of Nahalin was uneventful until a large contingent of Israeli security forces arrived, the organisers Protect the Harvest said in a statement.

“All volunteers were peacefully harvesting on the private land of a Palestinian family who had invited them. For reasons that remain unclear, the Israeli army showed up and detained approximately 80 people who were present.”

Soldiers said the area had been declared a closed military zone, separated the group by nationality and drove them to a nearby police station in minibuses for the Israelis and a larger bus for Americans.
Joshua Schoffman, who served as Israel’s deputy attorney general for more than a decade, described the mass detention as a “complete hallucination” in a post on social media.

“Just now, they told me that I’m being detained for the crime of olive harvesting,” he wrote. “We were asked to stop, and everyone complied. There was no friction whatsoever with settlers or with the security forces.”

Lander was released with a warning but all the others were still being held, Protect the Harvest said. Detainees include Jill Jacobs, the chief executive of T’ruah: The Rabbinic Call for Human Rights, and 11 other American rabbis affiliated with the group.
The detainees have been given water but no food. The Israeli military and police did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

On Monday, Lander made a first post about his journey to Palestine. “Our goals for the trip are to help protect the olive harvest – and to shed a light on the reality of the occupation,” he wrote. “Thankfully, our corner of today’s harvest was peaceful and successful. But violence unfortunately is never far away.”

articles.title: The night watch: the YouTubers who are guardians of a shark stuck in a South Korean canal
articles.summary: A group of self-appointed guardians wearing hi-vis and carrying selfie sticks watch over the animal that has been trapped for a month, drawing more than 1.6 million visitors
body: In South Korea, they call them jagyeongdan, a word whose meaning sits somewhere between vigilante group and neighbourhood watch. Each night they put on hi-vis vests, picked up their selfie sticks and gathered around the harbour in Busan to keep watch over an unlikely charge: a stranded shark affectionately known as Bukang-i.

On Wednesday, after more than a month in the canal and at the third attempt, the shark was successfully guided out, South Korea’s oceans ministry said. Officials expect her to move into open water in time.
For the month that she was stranded, the group of self-appointed guardians took turns to protect her, patrolling the waterfront at night for visitors who might disturb the animal.

Most are YouTubers who livestreamed the waterway, where the shark became a national celebrity. They stayed up through the night, calling out anyone shining torches or lasers into the water. Some of their videos have been watched hundreds of thousands of times.

“They bring fishing lamps, or the kind of lights people use at a campsite,” said Choi Won-jin, one of the shark’s protectors. He would arrive as the lights went out along the canal and wait for the offenders Koreans online call “lantern villains”.

The shark had been marooned in the canal since 18 September. Named after Bukhang, the Korean name for the city’s North Port, and about 3 metres long, the female dusky shark was one of a species classed as endangered worldwide. More than 1.6 million visitors came to see her, the city said, at a park that used to draw about 2,000 people on a busy Saturday.

Authorities had twice tried to guide her back out to sea and failed. Until she left, the shark remained in the canal, drawing crowds by day and leaving a handful of men to keep watch after dark. They patrolled the canal’s park to check everything was in order, ate snacks as the night went by, and shared their grievances on air about the behaviour they witnessed.

“We’re ordinary members of the public,” said Choi, who has had a YouTube channel for 10 years and covers trending issues in South Korea. “So we have no choice but to put it nicely, and get them to understand as best we can.”

“Don’t, please don’t switch the torch on,” said one of them, a YouTuber who lived nearby and went by the name Na Tae-soo. Most people complied, he said. “The animal thrashes about at night because of the torches, and it’s dangerous.”

His footage captured the shark twisting sharply away from a beam of light at 2am and striking the side of the canal. The national institute of fisheries science later confirmed an abrasion on her snout and said a visitor’s torch was likely to have startled the shark into injury.

Korean media reported that 105 officials from seven agencies watched over her, with a team on standby to reach the water within three minutes. Choi disputed this, saying that after dark it was almost up to him and the others.

The waterfront was closed to the public from midnight until 5am, a restriction the YouTubers said was impossible to enforce across a park that size. One night, livestreaming from the walkway, Choi filmed a man tipping food waste into the water.
Nobody saw the shark feed, though experts said feeding could happen in an instant and sharks her size did not need to eat often.
Further attempts to free the shark had been paused on the grounds that more force would distress her.

Cooler water had been expected to prompt her to move on. Dusky sharks prefer water between 18C and 26C, the fisheries institute said. Experts put 15C as the point below which her physiological functions would start to decline, and about 11C as the point at which survival would become precarious. Busan city officials had expected the canal to reach that temperature after the middle of November.

The fisheries institute recorded 46 large sharks off the east coast in the first half of this year, nearly four times as many as a year earlier, which it attributed to warmer seas and more of the fish that sharks feed on.

The affection for Bukang-i has meanwhile become an industry, with a commemorative soju, a baseball mascot in a shark cape and an honorary city ambassadorship, and nearby shops reporting a surge in sales. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, visited the canal in mid-October.
None of the shark’s guardians thought she should be forced out. Choi said the city should protect her where she was until she left of her own accord.

Kim Jong-hwan, who runs a small business, kept watch by day as well and livestreamed her almost every day. “I went to pass on information [to my followers], and after that I started observing her”, he said. “Watching her over time, with the water pumps being fired and then the nets, I came to find those things being done to her objectionable. So we ended up cheering her on.”

“She’s just an animal, and she came in by her own choice,” Kim said. “If it gets cold, if there’s no food, if the water doesn’t suit her, she’ll leave by herself. I’d like her to just be left alone, to rest there comfortably until then, and go.”

articles.title: ‘A powerful warning’: will Europe’s angry protests lead to real political change?
articles.summary: Hamstrung governments seem to have no answer to the public’s furious demands, making further discontent likely
body: In France, it was the piles of wheelie bins stacked up against school entrances that first hinted at the scale of student anger over crumbling classrooms and teacher shortages. In Spain, it was a tent camp that steadily grew in the heart of the capital as residents railed against soaring housing costs.
Similar scenes have since sprung up in Belgium, Italy and Portugal, and clashes have convulsed Albania’s capital of Tirana, hinting at an autumn of protests across Europe.

Much of the news coverage in recent days has focused on the violence that played out on the fringes of the protests in France and Italy. The protests themselves, however, point to what seems to be a diverse response to a common crisis: the growing perception, particularly among younger generations, that governments are unable, or unwilling, to deliver when it comes to affordable housing, social equality and robust public services.
“This is the most powerful warning from Europe’s angry youth today, in France and across the continent,” the policy analyst Alberto Alemanno said.

The framing stands in sharp contrast to the many rightwing and far-right voices who have sought to exploit the violence in France and Italy, linking it without evidence to migration while brushing over protesters’ wider demands.

Officials in France have dismissed any link between the violence and immigration. The country’s president, Emmanuel Macron, said on Sunday that the “unbridled violence” had been carried out by French people.

Alemanno, a professor of EU law at the HEC business school in Paris, said he had received an unprecedented number of calls from right-wing, xenophobic outlets in recent days, many of them seeking to fuel the idea of the protests as some sort of “pan-European revolt”.

It is a narrative that he describes as misleading. “The demonstrations have different causes and do not necessarily share political objectives,” he wrote this week. “Yet their rapid spread hints at a common weak point: too many young Europeans doubt that existing institutions can deliver the security, opportunity and voice they expect.”
The head of the Paris office of the European Council on Foreign Relations, Célia Belin, said some of those doubts were currently being reinforced in France.

“Faced with the high discontent of young people in high school, the government has no answer for them,” she said, citing an administration squeezed financially by a high deficit and debt-to-GDP ratio and limited politically by the country’s deadlocked parliament. “Basically the answer is: ‘There’s no money, there is nothing we can do.’ And that’s a huge problem.”

The view echoes that of the secretary general of France’s CGT union, Sophie Binet, after Saturday’s protests in which about half a million people turned up to rail against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services.

Binet condemned the violence, but she noted that the government had little choice when it came to quelling the protests. “Today’s mobilisation confirms the depth of the anger,” she said. “To get out of the crisis, there is only one way. Respond to the demands.”
Albania has also been shaken by mass student demonstrations for the past week after protests initially prompted by a proposal to build a resort backed by Donald Trump’s family.

In Milan, people took to the streets to protest against the rising cost of living, giving voice to the deep inequalities that now course through a city where an estimated one in 12 people is reportedly a millionaire.

In Lisbon’s Rossio Square, housing campaigners set up camp on Saturday surrounded by banners that read “homeless generation” and “I just want a home to live in” and vowing to stay on as long as possible. It was an echo of the protests that have sprung up in Porto in recent weeks as residents push back against housing prices that more than doubled between 2015 and 2024, rising roughly twice as fast as the EU average.

The managing director for Europe at the consulting firm Eurasia Group, Mujtaba Rahman, said what had burst into public view was not a single, coordinated European movement. Instead the events of recent days had laid bare a “convergence of distinct national protest movements”, each with substantially different triggers.

“What links them is a growing perception that European governments are unable to deliver affordable housing, functioning public services and economic security, particularly for younger generations,” he said, citing a growing gap between public expectations and governments’ fiscal capacity.
“This mismatch between political demands and economic reality is likely to remain and grow over time, which suggests further discontent and protests are likely over the medium term,” he said.

Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs and a former Spanish foreign minister, went a step further when asked this month about the similarities between the housing protests in Spain and the school protests in France.

“The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” she told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “Young French people are protesting for education, young Spanish people for housing, but in Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”

In Portugal, the campers were dislodged on Tuesday, leading to a fresh call for more housing protests. Similar calls for protests in the coming days have been heard across France, Spain and Italy, hinting at the tremendous task that lies ahead for officials across Europe, said Alemanno.

“They must protect peaceful demonstrators, hold those responsible for criminal acts accountable, and address the underlying pressures, from housing costs and insecure work to strained public services and an uncertain technological future,” he said.
“Europe’s democratic institutions will be judged not by how forcefully they condemn disorder, but by whether they can turn generational anger into tangible political change.”

articles.title: A student protest movement has gripped Serbia for two years. This weekend it will try to take power
articles.summary: Unorthodox campaign is challenging the ruling party’s 12-year reign with a bold democratic experiment
body: On a cool autumn evening, a team of Serbian student volunteers went canvassing in the housing estates of Krnjača, a Belgrade suburb. They were equipped with lanyards emblazoned with the word “victory”, a stock list of questions and a mobile app that mapped visited homes and the level of support in each.

The volunteers were part of a mass student movement, Student List, that has rocked Serbia with two years of constant protests. On Sunday, the group will represent the most serious challenge Aleksandar Vučić has faced in his 12 increasingly authoritarian years in power, by putting forward their own candidates in parliamentary elections.
They hope to emulate the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary six months ago, in a domino effect that could bring a democratic resurgence to central Europe.

Opinion polls have varied wildly, but many expert observers say a close race is quite possible, with neither side prepared to accept a loss as a legitimate result, raising the risk of post-election unrest and clashes.

In order to win, the students’ list of 250 candidates would have to break the mould of Serbian politics, along with Vučić’s grip on the country. He stepped down as president last month, five months before the end of his second and last term in office under the constitution, but only with the aim of extending his hold on power as prime minister at the head of his Serbian Progressive party (SNS).

In the section of the suburb assigned to them, law student Zak Veličković and campaign photographer Danijela Radojković were welcomed with overwhelming support. Apart from a small handful of polite doorstep rejections, from those claiming they had no interest in politics, people seized the opportunity to air their grievances.
Most promised their vote and a large minority offered help: some taxi drivers with flats in the low-rise apartment blocks said they would help ferry voters to the polling stations.
“Turnout is the key,” one said, adding: “Orbán fell with 80%” – a reference to the Hungarian elections in April.
Veličković began each conversation by asking what was the biggest problem in Serbian society, a query that often raised a laugh and replies such as: “How much time do you have?”

Corruption was the most frequent single complaint. On the corruption index run by Transparency International, Serbia ranks far worse than any of its neighbours, as the most corrupt country in Europe bar the dictatorships in Belarus and Russia.

There are frequent allegations of links between the SNS and organised crime, and the Student List’s slogan confronts that widespread perception head on, posing the question: “Serbia or Mafia?” The government denies all accusations and officially claims to be tackling organised crime.

The key local issues in Krnjača were the poor repair of the road bridge linking the suburb and central Belgrade, and the sewage system, which repeatedly fails in heavy rain, despite a personal promise by Vučić, who residents said had visited a few years earlier, to fix the problem.

The economy has been growing in recent years, but there is a widespread opinion that the fruits are not being fairly distributed. Porsche and Land Rover car showrooms have been established in Krnjača but public spaces look neglected. Some of Belgrade’s trams are more than 50 years old.

It was a major infrastructure failure that sparked the student protests – the collapse of a concrete canopy in Novi Sad railway station on 1 November 2024, killing 16 people. Evidence pointed to botched modifications made during refurbishment work, but so far there has been no official finding on the cause, and no official has been held accountable.
When Belgrade students blocked a road in a vigil for the victims three weeks after the disaster, they were attacked by a SNS mob and the protest movement went nationwide.

The students initially distanced themselves from opposition parties and avoided any kind of hierarchy or conventional leadership structure. That was partly an ideological choice and partly practical. The SNS and state-run media rule in part through smearing opponents and the student’s collective approach offered fewer targets.

Vučić rose to prominence in the 1990s as a radical nationalist, who supported the policies of Serbian expansion and ethnic cleansing led by Slobodan Milošević, who died of a heart attack in detention in The Hague during his trial on charges of genocide and crimes against humanity committed in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo. He served as Milošević’s information minister throughout the Kosovo conflict. As president, Vučić has not emulated his predecessor’s militarism, but he has maintained his nationalist playbook in domestic politics, dismissing the opposition as stooges of unspecified foreign powers.

So far those well-worn tactics have proved ineffective against the students. A survey published in July by a Serbian pro-democracy group, the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA) and Stanford University showed significantly more support for the students (45%) than for the SNS (36%), but that was well before Vučić announced his resignation on 27 September and his election machine went into top gear. Other, more recent domestic polls show the SNS in the lead, though the pollsters in question are seen by the opposition as pro-government.

Vučić himself shows signs he is taking the political threat seriously enough to throw himself into the campaign, making 129 live television appearances in August, more than four times the previous month’s total.

“Serbia has been an electoral autocracy and in electoral autocracies only ruling political parties can win,” Raša Nedeljkov, CRTA’s programme director, said. But he added that the status quo was now in jeopardy.

“What we are seeing in the past days, weeks, months, is that strength; the homogeneous government that Vučić used to have is no longer there. He is faced with a completely unorthodox political actor and the toolbox that he has improved over the years since he came to power is no longer effective.”

Unable to crush the students by force, division or denigration, Vučić gambled, announcing his resignation as president and calling snap elections, in the apparent hope of catching the students off guard, but they responded by improvising a democratic experiment.

The 250 candidates were mostly nominated by university faculties (there are more than 160 doctorates among them) with a sprinkling of farmers and other professions, and each candidate was subject to approval by plenary sessions of the student protests.
Related: French schoolchildren have been treated like enemies to be crushed – for telling the truth | Rokhaya Diallo

The policy platform has also been decided by plenum, with the result that divisive issues, especially foreign policy, have been played down: the question of future EU membership has been left to a referendum and Kosovo is claimed as an integral part of Serbia.
One of the chosen candidates, Milica Jovanović, an assistant professor at the University of Belgrade, argued the List’s lack of political experience was not necessarily a drawback.

“We are political amateurs, but we are experts,” Jovanović said. “We are people who have led projects, led organisations, led our community, and actually I cannot see that we can do worse than these politicians … The only thing that matters is willingness to improve something, expertise to actually do it and support to do the actual change.”

The Student List is pitted against the political monolith of the SNS, in power for 14 years and with control of the state apparatus. It has accused the foreign ministry of rigging the diaspora vote by keeping polling stations open where support for Vučić is strong, such as the Serbian part of Bosnia, while closing them in parts of North America where the opposition could expect to perform well. The ministry did not respond to a request to comment.

The SNS grip on national media is meanwhile evident everywhere. A CRTA survey in September found that 69% of air time on Serbian television channels was dedicated to the ruling majority. Of the remaining coverage of the opposition, 42% was negative in tone and 53% neutral.

The student movement has sought to sidestep government domination of the media by, it says, going door to door, including sending a canvasser “to every village”, in the hope of making inroads into Vučić’s solid base in the Serbian countryside. The outcome could hinge on whether these student emissaries can change rural minds.

No SNS officials responded to a request for comment. Gordana Čomić, a former member of the opposition Democratic party who served as a minister in the SNS government, said the students were exaggerating the extent of their rural campaign and were deluded if they thought they could win.

“They are not in the field. It’s propaganda. They have no clue who their voters are,” Čomić said, predicting that the Student List would win about 80 of the 250 seats in the national assembly and then dissipate.
“They won’t have a clue what’s their role there. How will they work when they don’t want to talk with anyone from the ruling parties? They will just dissolve.”

Radivoje Grujić, a Serbian electoral consultant based in Warsaw, was also sceptical that the Student List could make gains in the countryside and argued the students’ only path to victory would be if the Novi Sad disaster mobilised Serbians who had previously stayed away from politics.

“These people were saying: I’m not involved in politics, and then politics got them killed,” he said. “This definitely triggered a lot of people to get involved and obviously those people will not vote for Vučić. I think that’s the only chance for a change – that reservoir of votes of people who never voted.”
In a close race, other factors are expected to come into play. Minority parties representing ethnic Hungarians, Bosniaks and Albanians could emerge as kingmakers.

Previous elections have seen multiple allegations of various forms of rigging, including vote-buying, voter intimidation and ballot box stuffing, so the Student List is planning to deploy an unprecedented number of opposition monitors on Sunday.

That could in turn raise the prospect of election day clashes. Attacks on opposition representatives by gangs of anonymous, black-clad burly men has been a frequent feature of SNS rule. In the days before the elections, one of those hired thugs has turned whistleblower.

“My role was to lead a group of guys to the riskiest and most critical places, to any gatherings where students or the opposition were on the other side,” Momcilo Marjanovic told the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network, saying that he was covertly paid through a fictitious job at a public utility.
“It was our job, as a last resort of course, to use force, although it often happened not as a last resort.”

Diplomats in Belgrade thought that Vučić’s plans to host a major international event, EXPO 2027, next year, could constrain any violence. If his hold on power is threatened, Vučić also has the option of forcing repeated recounts in the hope that the students’ momentum may eventually dissipate.
The movement is determined that will not happen and has focused its planning in recent weeks on post-election street tactics to defend any victory.
“I think there is a strong feeling of now or never,” Jelena Kleut, an associate professor of media studies, said at a recent demonstration outside the education ministry in Belgrade.
“I think that people have really felt in their skin what the regime is capable of and there is a sense you still need to stay strong because the job is not finished.”

articles.title: Wednesday briefing: ​Why has Jackdaw been approved in the middle of a climate crisis?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: The government has approved drilling in the Jackdaw gas field despite fierce opposition and evidence against it
body: Good morning. After weeks of speculation, the secretary of state for energy and net zero, Miatta Fahnbulleh, approved drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield this morning. In a statement, published a few minutes before today’s First Edition, Fahnbulleh stressed that the government remains “resolute” in achieving net zero by 2050. It has also announced a new wealth fund that will invest tax revenues from North Sea oil and gas into low-carbon projects.

Even so, Fahnbulleh’s decision will be a monumental disappointment for climate campaigners (and I’d bet many readers of First Edition, too). So this morning’s newsletter is about two things: why the government approved Jackdaw, despite all of the arguments marshalled against it, and, in an attempt to strike a more hopeful note, what it can do to reduce the UK’s reliance on fossil fuels. That’s after the headlines.
UK news | During the Covid-19 pandemic, and government failures caused the virus to spread “like wildfire” among vulnerable and elderly people, a public inquiry has found.

Europe news | Italy’s government is sending 500 soldiers to Milan and vowed a “firm response from the state” after protests against the cost of living descended into clashes with police, vandalism and looting.
Ukraine | The US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv about Russian missile strikes, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after a meeting with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway.
Media | Television channels BBC Three and BBC Scotland are to close and the Radio 4 Extra radio station will be scrapped, as part of the corporation’s drive to cut £500m in costs.
UK news | RAF Typhoon fighters are to be used in efforts to protect Saudi Arabia from attack by Yemen’s Houthis, as western allies increase their intervention in the escalating conflict.

First, a quick recap: Jackdaw is a gasfield in the North Sea, 150 miles from Aberdeen. In 2022, the Conservative government gave consent to Adura, a joint venture between Shell and the Norwegian state giant Equinor, to produce gas there. Last year, this consent was blocked by campaigners who challenged it in a judicial review. The companies were forced to resubmit their applications with new information about the climate impact of the gas they would produce at Jackdaw. Fahnbulleh has now approved this application.

The other site that Fahnbulleh is also considering is Rosebank, a new oilfield 80 miles off the Shetland coast, although a decision on that has not yet been made. Jackdaw, a small gasfield, was always going to be an easier sell than the far larger Rosebank, which would produce seven times the carbon emissions if it was approved, and some environmental campaigners regard the sole approval of Jackdaw as an acceptable compromise.

Even so, Jackdaw’s impact on UK gas supplies will be minimal. Uplift and Greenpeace, the NGOs that challenged the 2022 consent, estimate that Jackdaw will provide just 2% of the UK’s gas over its lifespan, doing “next to nothing” to reduce reliance on foreign gas imports (though together with Rosebank, it could account for up to 10% of the UK’s gas production). Gas production in the North Sea is set to fall 99% by 2050. Even if the government approved new licenses for drilling in the North Sea (something Labour has said it won’t do), this figure would only decrease to 97%. “It’s geology determining this decline, not politics,” the Guardian’s environment editor, Fiona Harvey, tells me.
Why is the government approving Jackdaw?

Many arguments have been made in favour of drilling in the North Sea. Few have survived contact with reality. Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch have both claimed it will reduce oil and gas prices (it won’t) and improve energy security (this also doesn’t hold true). The most persuasive arguments for Jackdaw are that it will boost UK tax revenues, stem the loss of jobs from North Sea oil, and that since the UK already relies so much on natural gas, approving Jackdaw will have no meaningful impact on UK emissions. Put simply, if the UK isn’t getting gas from Jackdaw, we’ll simply buy it somewhere else. In its statement this morning, the government stressed that Jackdaw won’t prevent the UK from meeting its legally binding limits on carbon emissions.

But these arguments are also flawed. Only 27 direct, full-time jobs would be created by Jackdaw, and tax revenues from the North Sea are falling. The government estimates the industry will generate £4.1bn in tax revenue from 2025-2026, but much of this is negated by the £3.26bn it will spend on tax relief and support for the industry. And ultimately, approving more gas production at Jackdaw means the global supply of fossil fuels will increase. There’s a somewhat technical question about whether a surplus of fossil fuels leads to greater carbon emissions. As the Guardian’s energy correspondent, Jillian Ambrose, points out, emissions are driven by energy consumption, not energy production.

And yet there’s a reason that climate campaigners argue that governments and fossil fuel companies ought to “keep it in the ground!” Actively preventing the exploitation of fossil fuel assets – or “stranding” them, in the lingo – guarantees the prevention of future emissions. “When you interrogate each of the arguments in favour of Jackdaw, they reveal the power of the oil and gas lobby behind them,” Matthew Taylor, the Guardian’s environment correspondent, tells me.
If Jackdaw has no meaningful impact on UK carbon emissions, what would?

The answer to this is pretty straightforward: one of the best ways of reducing the UK’s emissions is by tackling its reliance on gas. About 85% of homes still rely on gas boilers, and just 2% of UK homes are heated with electric heat pumps, one of the lowest rates in Europe. Previous policies to increase insulation have been either short-lived or disastrous. The Green Homes Grant promised by Boris Johnson’s government in 2020 was cut after just six months. The Energy Company programme run by the last Conservative government left 98% of homes with external wall insulation needing work to resolve “major issues” (pdf) with damp and mould.

More recently, the UK’s warm homes plan introduced by Starmer’s government pledged to invest £15bn in upgrading 5m homes. Climate campaigners were somewhat sceptical about aspects of this plan, including its focus on green technologies rather than the more prosaic subject of loft insulation, and the government’s decision to quietly ditch a ban on gas boilers by 2035.

“Boiler companies and plumbers have made a very good living from slinging out gas boilers day after day,” Fiona says. (Anyone who has spoken to their plumber about installing a heat pump, only to be met with vehement grumbling, will probably be nodding their head at this point.) “These companies could start making heat pumps. They know how to do it. And they could train their installers.” This seems increasingly unlikely, particularly since ministers have recently been looking at slashing the heat pump subsidy for UK households, something that Treasury mandarins consider a “middle-class” luxury.
How else can the government address the loss of jobs in fossil fuel sectors?

Funny you should ask! The headline figure of 27 jobs should be treated with a degree of scepticism, because there will also be a wider impact on supply chains and roles created in temporary construction. Still, “even with the government allowing Jackdaw to go ahead, any job gains will be outweighed by long-term decline,” Fiona says. Nobody thinks Jackdaw will have a big impact on employment – not even North Sea oil workers themselves.

The more optimistic argument for creating a small number of jobs in an industry that is rapidly shrinking is that it will slow the pace at which the North Sea is shedding workers whose skills will be needed in the green transition. “Slowing the decline of employment in the North Sea would make for a smoother transition from fossil fuels to green activity,” Jillian says.

One way of boosting employment while decoupling UK homes from fossil fuels could be funding a massive retrofitting programme. Fiona recently covered the findings from a thinktank, E3G, that suggested a programme focused on insulating homes and investing in heat pumps would create about 50,000 new jobs spread across thousands of small businesses, and help alleviate the cost of living by slashing energy bills. “The problem is, this isn’t sexy, and there’s no big fossil fuel lobby behind it,” Matthew says. “But it would be the sane thing to do, to improve people’s energy security, reduce bills, and create good, well-paid jobs. It’s a no-brainer.”

“Burnham faces climate revolt after approval of North Sea gas drilling”, is the Guardian’s front page today.

The Telegraph has “Teachers face ban on Palestine badges”, Times leads with “Mahmood’s fight to save her migrant crackdown”. The FT runs “AI debt nerves trigger race for default insurance in case boom turns to bust”, the Mirror has “Tories’ cruel Covid car home ‘lie’”, and the i Paper says “Man City paid council £750,000 a year for stadium naming rights – that sold for £100m”.

On Prince Harry, the Sun splashes “I want to work it out … some people don’t”, the Mail writes “Oh, do put a sock in it Harry!”, and the Express has “Harry’s ‘some people don’t want it to work out’ dig”.
Helen Haines loses leg after being attacked with car

A man has been charged after the Australian MP Helen Haines was allegedly attacked with a car outside her electorate office in the state of Victoria. Haines, who is an independent MP, has lost one leg as a result of the incident and surgeons were fighting on Tuesday to save the other leg. Police say 43-year-old Brendan Nugent has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Annie Kelly speaks to Guardian Australia political editor Tom McIlroy.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Ghent’s new €20m (£17m) design museum is a gleaming monument to recycling. Designed by London-based architects Carmody Groarke, it was built using everything from car windscreens, seaweed and old toilets to rubble dug straight from the building site.

Its bricks, many of which were pressed by the public during a two-day festival, are made of pulverised construction waste and hydrated lime. As well as saving two-thirds of the embodied carbon of a regular fired clay brick, they will continue to absorb CO2 from the atmosphere in the coming years, as the lime cures.

“We’re not claiming this is … a solution to the climate crisis,” says Sian Ricketts, Carmody Groarke’s sustainability lead. “But it is a sort of 82,000-brick proof of concept that you can do something different.”

articles.title: Battle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensifies days before Brazil presidential runoff
articles.summary: Lula’s supporters suspect tech firm meddling on behalf of US president Donald Trump, who has close ties to Bolsonaro family
body: Five days after his defeat in the first round of the Brazilian presidential election, leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spent almost 24 hours unable to boost his Instagram posts, while his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, could.

Lula’s lawyers included the episode in a list of incidents that they submitted to the electoral court and international observers as “evidence” that Meta, Instagram’s owner, was actively trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour.

Reports from Lula supporters saying their content had been removed or its reach restricted flooded social media in Brazil, while about a dozen watchdogs and research groups published reports describing what they called “indications” that Meta may have favoured the senator’s campaign.
Meta called Lula’s allegations “false and unfounded”, saying there had been “technical incidents” that affected campaigns from “different parts of the political spectrum”.

The controversy fuelled the electoral battle between Lula and Bolsonaro just days before next Sunday’s runoff and gained further traction after the electoral court ordered Meta not to give the candidates “unequal treatment”.
Related: Brazil cuts work week to 40 hours in win for Lula ahead of runoff

Late last week, justice Marco Aurélio Bellizze said he had found no evidence of deliberate action by the company, which would require further investigation, but he gave Meta 24 hours to prove that the problems affecting Lula had been fixed and would not happen again.

On Monday, after saying the company had failed to do so, Bellizze gave Meta a further 24 hours. The company responded on Tuesday, again denying any favouritism and saying it had introduced human review to prevent any automated restrictions.

Meta’s oversight board, a quasi-independent body whose decisions are binding, issued a statement saying it was “concerned by recurring enforcement failures in Meta’s election integrity efforts”, citing both Brazil’s election and the suspension of the anti-Trump No Kings movement’s account in the US for several hours last Saturday, during demonstrations aimed at encouraging early voting in the midterm elections.
The company said it suspended the No Kings account after its anti-fraud systems wrongly flagged what they believed was bot traffic, and apologised.

The board said it had seen the same pattern in Brazil, where there had been an “over-enforcement of Meta’s fraud policies against Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s ad accounts” on 23 September, when his campaign advertising account was disabled for more than an hour. Meta said this had happened “by mistake … and not for political reasons” after an anti-fraud review wrongly classified an ad as an attempt to impersonate a government social programme.

The board said: “From the removal of political activist accounts during protests in the US ahead of the midterm elections to technical restrictions that hit the accounts of a presidential candidate in Brazil leading to allegations of electoral interference, it’s clear that Meta must do more to ensure that its enforcement practices during elections are transparent and consistent, and that political speech is protected rather than stifled”.

João Victor Archegas, the coordinator at the thinktank Institute for Technology and Society, said it was “almost impossible” to prove any interference by Meta in Brazilian elections because only the company has access to its internal data, meaning there is no real external scrutiny, either from the electoral court or from the watchdogs producing reports on it.

“What we have so far is a collection of cases that perhaps one day we can piece together and reach some conclusion one way or the other. But today, because of the lack of information, unfortunately we cannot be certain,” he said.

Platforms such as Google and TikTok are not allowing political advertising in this election, leaving Meta’s services as the only large-scale channels for paid digital campaigning, which so far has earned the company £43m, 85% more than it made during the last presidential election.

A report by the watchdog CTRL+Z, founded by a former executive at Meta’s WhatsApp, catalogued 1,121 reports of lost or suppressed reach, restrictions on reposting, and account bans and blocks affecting mostly leftwing profiles. Meta dismissed it as a catalogue of anecdotes and users’ perceptions.

Media outlets posted examples of an experiment in which WhatsApp’s AI assistant refused to generate artwork featuring “Lula” and his ballot number, but did so for “Flávio” – Brazilians widely refer to the senator by his first name, reserving the surname for his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro.
The company said this reflected “a specific gap in our safeguards, not political bias” and that AI artwork could be generated using Lula’s first name, Luiz, with his ballot number.

Many Lula supporters raised suspicions that Meta was allegedly acting on behalf of the US president, Donald Trump, who has close ties to the Bolsonaro family and whom Lula has accused of trying to interfere in Brazil’s election.
Related: Lula says Trump wants to ‘colonise’ and capture Brazil’s resources by meddling in election

Lula’s lawyers appeared to embrace that argument, describing Meta in their filing to the electoral court as a “foreign company aligned with the Trump administration” that was acting as a “vector of external pressure on the [Brazilian] electorate”, without, however, offering any evidence of possible US involvement.

In the 9 October episode in which Lula’s campaign was temporarily unable to boost posts on Instagram, which 70% of Brazilian adults say they use as their primary source of information, his lawyers said that “silencing” the incumbent’s social media while his opponent’s continued operating normally created an unfair advantage for Bolsonaro.

The company said the problem affected only new posts, while older ones could still be promoted, and that it had been a “global outage” affecting “thousands of advertisers in different countries”, though Bolsonaro’s campaign was not among them.

Meta added: “We apply the same rules to all candidates, parties and political viewpoints in Brazil, just as we do in elections around the world. We do not suppress content to harm one side or give preferential treatment to any side.”

NetLab, a research laboratory on the internet and social media at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, produced a report showing that Meta allowed at least 1,600 election ads to be boosted from outside Brazil, something prohibited under Brazilian law.

Débora Salles, NetLab’s general coordinator, said they had not identified political bias towards either side, but that the failure “shows how the company repeatedly fails to ensure safety and compliance with electoral law”.

On the eve of the vote, NetLab identified paid ads that posed as official posts from the electoral court and contained false information that encouraged abstention, claiming that if it was raining, voters could cast their ballots online, which is not possible in Brazil.

“Regardless of whether a candidacy is being helped or harmed, what we see is that the company has difficulty complying with Brazilian electoral law and ends up undermining the integrity of the electoral process,” said Salles.

articles.title: Residents of ‘1066 Country’ lose battle for Bayeux tapestry tickets
articles.summary: Exclusive: East Sussex MP Helena Dollimore says ‘shambolic’ museum phone line has made her constituents lose out to ‘queue jumpers’
body: Hastings residents have missed out on tickets for the Bayeux tapestry after being put on hold for hours by a “glitchy and shambolic” phone system, their MP has said.

People from “1066 Country” were promised a chance to buy before a sales line opened to the public on Wednesday. But Helena Dollimore, the MP for Hastings and Rye, said it has been almost impossible for her constituents to get through to the British Museum.

VIP guests including Maya Jama, Mick Jagger and senior staff at Samsung and Bloomberg have had no such issues gaining access to Bayeux viewings, having attended star-studded events held in the tapestry room since September.

Hastings residents were told they could get early access to book the latest release of tickets from Monday this week by calling the British Museum box office and providing proof of their address. But Dollimore said her constituents were left on hold for hours.
“Why do my constituents have to work on a glitchy phone line when online booking is clearly possible for others?” she asked.
“One person booked after two hours and 38 minutes in the queue, another said he was on hold for two and a half hours.
“If you can’t get access right for the people in the place this tapestry tells the story of, you need to sort that out before you start letting people jump the queue.”

Celebrities, businesspeople and politicians flocked to the museum on Saturday for a ball. The guest of honour, tech billionaire Igor Tulchinsky, posed next to Rosanna Konarzewski, a communications executive who was wearing a sweeping ballgown made of a replica Bayeux tapestry. Sources in attendance said that while the general public have been banned from taking pictures of the embroidery, some ball guests managed to photograph it.

The Guardian revealed that another tech billionaire, Peter Thiel, was given a VIP tour of the embroidery before it opened to the public. Guests of the One Aldwych hotel are also allowed to view the tapestry if they book a £1,000-a-night room.

Dollimore said: “I had a constituent who waited for hours with her elderly parent who was in her 80s, and they were sent away because of a corporate event. They promised the people of 1066 Country would be able to get access to the tapestry, but seem to be prioritising these corporates.”
The MP has unsuccessfully tried to get tickets for herself and her family. “I have been trying since 10am to get through, and even I can’t,” she said.
The MP managed to secure access to the tapestry for schoolchildren across Hastings after lobbying the museum. “To be fair to the museum, that has been a success,” she said.

Members of the public faced online queues of up to nine hours when tickets went on sale for the first time this summer. There were reports of 40,000 people queueing by mid-morning, with that figure ballooning to almost 80,000 by mid-afternoon.
The 70-metre (229ft) tapestry, which is made of linen with embroidered images of events surrounding the Battle of Hastings in 1066, arrived in the UK in July for the first time in nearly 1,000 years.
Adult tickets cost £33 in peak hours and £27 at other times, compared with the €12 (£10) fee at the artwork’s home in Bayeux, Normandy.

A British Museum spokesperson said: “Demand for the Bayeux tapestry exhibition has been exceptionally high. In recognition of the area’s historic connection to the Battle of Hastings we agreed to offer residents the chance to secure tickets before their wider release.
“This offer is not guaranteed access – it is on a first-come, first-served basis in the same way tickets for the exhibition are on sale to our members and the public.
“All residents are still able to book tickets as part of the general sale on 21 October and will have further opportunities in the new year when the third tranche of tickets are released.”
• This article was amended on 21 October 2026. An earlier version incorrectly described Rosanna Konarzewski as the “host” of a Bayeux tapestry ball held at the British Museum.
